paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1968, the ecologist Garrett Hardin published an essay entitled The Tragedy of the Commons, in which he argued that resources owned by everyone will inevitably be overexploited. His illustration was a shared pasture: each herder gains the full benefit of adding one more animal, while the cost of overgrazing is shared among all. Rational self-interest, therefore, leads to ruin. The essay became one of the most cited in the social sciences, and it was invoked to justify two solutions: privatisation or central government control.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The political scientist Elinor Ostrom challenged this conclusion on empirical grounds. Studying communities from Swiss mountain villages to Japanese forests and Spanish irrigation systems, she found many examples of people managing shared resources successfully for centuries, without privatisation and without external control. Hardin's herders, she pointed out, were imaginary individuals who cannot communicate. Real communities talk, make rules and punish cheats. For this work, she became in 2009 the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Economics.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: From her case studies, Ostrom distilled design principles that distinguish durable arrangements. Boundaries must be clear, so that it is known who may use the resource. Rules must fit local conditions and be made with the participation of those affected. Monitoring should be carried out by users themselves or by people accountable to them, and sanctions should begin mild and escalate with repeated offences. Finally, there must be accessible means of resolving conflicts. Where these conditions were absent, commons were more likely to fail.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Critics point out that Ostrom's examples tend to involve small, stable communities with a long shared history, and that her principles may not scale to global problems like climate change, where the relevant community is the whole of humanity, without a common authority. This is a fair objection, though some scholars note that Ostrom herself advocated polycentric governance, in which action takes place at several levels simultaneously, from neighbourhoods to international agreements, rather than relying on a single global solution.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Hardin's essay was not worthless. It drew attention to a real danger, and there are indeed commons that have collapsed, such as many ocean fisheries. But it presented a possible outcome as an inevitable one. The more important lesson of Ostrom's work is that the choice is not binary. Between the market and the state lies a large territory of cooperation, and the fate of a shared resource depends less on who owns it than on whether those who use it can organise themselves.
